sourceSaysEdits.says: Reports undisputed Pauline authorship, a usual date of 53–57 CE at Ephesus reached with the help of Acts (Barrett links 16:5–10 to Acts 19:22), Papyrus 46, the earlier letter of 5:9, the 6:20 addition, the Western placement of 14:34–35, Fitzmyer's report that most commentators now treat those verses as an interpolation and the main views against that, partition theories, the Greek literary source of 15:33, and 15:29.

Treats 6:12–13, 7:1, 8:1, and 8:4 as Corinthian slogans while noting debate over 6:13 and 6:18; gives lexicon meanings for the words in 6:9; sets out the margin-gloss case against 14:34–35 and argues the verses are original; prefers boast at 13:3 with Papyrus 46; notes that the covering of 11:10 is not specified; identifies 15:33 as a line of Menander; and explains the Aramaic of 16:22.

Reports that influential 18th–19th-century commentators upheld head covering as normative, that some mid-twentieth-century scholarship read 11:3–16 as culturally specific, that most Western evangelical churches now give the practice little emphasis while some traditions keep it, and that a 1965 interpretation takes long hair as the covering, against which others point to the different Greek words in 11:15 and 11:6–7.

Describes the dispute over whether spiritual gifts ceased with the apostolic age, its Reformed origins, the historic continuationism of Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist and other traditions, the main cessationist arguments, and the competing readings of 13:8–12, including cessationists who share the eschatological reading.

Describes the painful visit, the anguished letter and competing apostles whom Paul called false apostles and super-apostles; says scholars disagree on when the parts were written, yet the letter can reasonably be read as a coherent whole.

Describes the papyrus codex of Paul's letters, split between the Chester Beatty Library and the University of Michigan, with 2 Corinthians between 1 Corinthians and Ephesians, a leaf holding 11:33–12:9, and lines lost at the foot of every leaf; its date rests on handwriting, with most proposals from the late second to the third century, sometimes about 200.

sourceSaysEdits.says: Recounts the death of James the brother of the Lord, quotes Hegesippus that he was called the Just, quotes Josephus on his death after Festus died, and says James is said to be the author of the first of the so-called catholic epistles, which is disputed because not many of the ancients mention it, though it was read publicly in very many churches.

Surveys traditional, two-stage and pseudonymous views of authorship; lists grounds given for the pseudonymous view (polished Greek, possible dependence on 1 Peter, possible response to Paul or his followers, late attestation) and its late-first to mid-second-century dating; gives 62 CE for James's death; lists early manuscripts; reports Athanasius's list of 367 and Luther's moving James toward the end of his Bible; summarizes views that James answers Paul, answers a misunderstanding of Paul, or does not have Paul in view. The article carries a 2026 notice about suspected machine-written text.

Philip Schaff's 1910 history reports that Luther found it impossible to harmonize James and Paul on justification, called James an epistle of straw because it had no evangelical character, and in his New Testament prefaces judged James unfavorably and changed the traditional order. It is a report, not Luther's own preface.

findings.briefingText: The book calls itself a revelation, a prophecy, and a letter in its first eleven verses.
findings.evidence: 1:1 ("This is the Revelation of Jesus Christ"), 1:3 ("words of the prophecy"), 1:4 ("John, to the seven assemblies... Grace to you and peace"), 1:11 ("write in a book and send to the seven assemblies")
findings.problem: The book calls itself a revelation (1:1) and a prophecy (1:3) and uses a letter greeting and address (1:4, 1:11), but it does not call itself a "letter" (unlike textualHistory[0], which accurately says it "takes the form of a letter").

findings.briefingText: It glosses two Hebrew names for its readers, Abaddon (9:11) and Harmagedon (16:16)
findings.evidence: 9:11 ("His name in Hebrew is 'Abaddon', but in Greek, he has the name 'Apollyon'"), 16:16 ("He gathered them together into the place which is called in Hebrew, 'Harmagedon'.")
findings.problem: At 16:16 the text merely labels "Harmagedon" as a Hebrew name without glossing or translating its meaning, and at 9:11 it gives a Greek equivalent rather than a gloss of the Hebrew word's sense.

findings.briefingText: A fragment known as Papyrus 18, dated about 300, preserves 1:4–7.
findings.evidence: Not visible in the hosted text, and none of the briefing's sources entries mentions Papyrus 18 in its says line.
findings.problem: The claim about Papyrus 18 (P.Oxy. 1079, dated around 300 CE, preserving Revelation 1:4–7) is true, but it is unsupported by any of the briefing's listed sources.

findings.problem: This concrete historical claim lacks support in the hosted text and the briefing's source descriptions; I believe it is doubtful as stated.

findings.briefingText: Clement of Alexandria and Origen denied an earthly millennium, Dionysius of Alexandria held that the book could not be read literally, and Augustine's later adoption of this reading made it widespread.
findings.evidence: The wikipedia-millennialism says line names Origen and Dionysius as early opponents of an earthly millennium and notes Augustine's adoption, but it is not described as saying anything about Clement of Alexandria or that Dionysius held the whole book could not be read literally.
findings.problem: The Clement claim is unsupported by the briefing's source descriptions, and the Dionysius claim is broader than the described source; I am unsure about Clement as stated.

findings.briefingText: These are figures for communities, cities, and loyalty, in the prophets' language, not a verdict on women as such.
findings.evidence: Rev 2:20 presents Jezebel as a woman at Thyatira who “calls herself a prophetess” and teaches the servants, while Rev 14:4 has also been read as referring to literally celibate male virgins as well as symbolically.
findings.problem: The sentence presents only the figurative reading for all the passages and omits the major alternatives that Jezebel was a real teacher given a symbolic name and that 14:4 may be literal.

findings.briefingText: The lemma ἑπτά occurs 55 times in the SBL Greek of Revelation, 11 of them in chapter 1.
findings.evidence: The briefing repeatedly uses “lemma” for Greek words but nowhere explains that a lemma is the dictionary or headword form under which inflected forms are counted.
findings.problem: A first-time reader cannot follow what is being counted or why the count differs from counting one exact printed form.

findings.briefingText: Many modern scholars link 666 to a Hebrew-letter spelling of Nero Caesar;
findings.evidence: Rev 13:18 tells the reader to “calculate the number of the beast,” but the briefing never explains that Hebrew letters could also function as numbers or how a spelling of Nero Caesar would produce 666.
findings.problem: A newcomer cannot follow how a Hebrew spelling of a name becomes the number 666 without an explanation of that letter-number practice.
